dedupe_keys.name: heat moderating effects of bus stop shelters and tree shade on ridership in austin texas

description: This study by K. Lanza and C. P. Durand, published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2021, tests whether bus stop shelters and tree canopy around stops moderate the effect of warm season temperatures on ridership in Austin, Texas, and whether they are equitably distributed. Coverage: boardings per bus at 2,271 stops of the Capital Metropolitan Transportation Authority from 1 April to 30 September 2019; air temperature from the Camp Mabry weather station; tree canopy classified from high-resolution National Agriculture Imagery Program imagery; race, ethnicity, poverty, median age and bus commuters by census tract from the 2014-2018 American Community Survey; multilevel negative binomial regression. Shelters did not moderate the effect of high temperatures, while each one-percent increase in tree canopy was associated with a slightly smaller drop in ridership; shelters and trees were generally equitably distributed. Format and access: an open article on PubMed Central. Licence and cost: free under CC BY 4.0. Caveats: small effects that the authors link to riders' transit dependency. The canopy and ridership relations can inform stop shading in extreme heat climate adaptation and exposure models. It relates to CapMetro vehicle location data and NAIP imagery in the catalogue.

name: Heat-moderating effects of bus stop shelters and tree shade on ridership in Austin, Texas
outcomes: Shelters did not moderate the effect of high temperatures on ridership; each one-percent increase in tree canopy was associated with a smaller ridership decrease during high temperatures (1.6% against 1.7%); shelters and trees were generally equitably distributed.
